strengths: Novel and timely perspective: The paper formalizes an underexplored economic vulnerability in LLM-as-a-service, viewing tokenization through the lens of a principal-agent problem and mechanism design.

Solid theoretical contributions: The paper provides clear formal proofs showing that finding the longest plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k sampling is NP-hard (via reduction from the Hamiltonian path problem) and characterizes all additive incentive-compatible pricing schemes (Theorem 6).

Effective proof-of-concept: Algorithm 1 demonstrates that even though optimal misreporting is computationally hard, a simple heuristic based on BPE token splitting can still systematically overcharge users (up to ~13%) while remaining strictly within the plausible top-p sampling envelope.

Clear writing and well-structured presentation: The narrative flows logically from unconstrained misreporting, to auditability and computational hardness, to heuristic vulnerability, and finally to incentive-compatible mechanism design (pay-per-character).
weaknesses: Practical threat model caveats: For models with public tokenizers (e.g., standard BPE vocabularies used by OpenAI via `tiktoken` or open-weights tokenizers), client-side SDKs and knowledgeable users can easily run canonical tokenizer encoding on the received text string. While the paper correctly notes that tokenization is not mathematically unique and alternative valid paths exist in autoregressive generation, in practice users might expect canonical greedy BPE segmentations; the paper would benefit from explicitly addressing this canonicalization defense.

Sensitivity to sampling parameters: The empirical overcharging gains with Algorithm 1 are evaluated primarily at higher temperatures (e.g., 1.15 to 1.45) and loose sampling thresholds (p=0.99). For common production defaults (e.g., temperature 0.0 to 0.7, p=0.9), the plausible search space narrows significantly and the overcharging margin drops to <0.5%, limiting the practical exploitability in deterministic or near-deterministic settings.

Cost mismatch under pay-per-character: In transformer architectures, hardware compute and memory bandwidth scale strictly with token counts (due to the autoregressive step structure), not characters. Under a fixed pay-per-character mechanism, providers bear financial risk on inputs/outputs with unusually low character-to-token ratios (e.g., code, non-Latin scripts, dense symbolic math); the paper could expand further on how this operational risk could be mitigated.

strengths: Novel and insightful conceptual framing: The paper identifies a blind spot in current LLM-as-a-service pricing models, specifically the moral hazard arising from the non-uniqueness of string tokenization under pay-per-token contracts.

Solid theoretical foundation: The authors rigorously frame the problem within principal-agent theory, prove the NP-hardness of finding the optimal plausible tokenization via a reduction from Hamiltonian Path (and extend it to top-k and probability threshold settings), and derive a crisp characterization of additive incentive-compatible mechanisms.

Practical demonstration of vulnerability: The paper designs a concrete, computationally lightweight heuristic (Algorithm 1) that empirically achieves non-trivial overcharging (up to ~13%) while satisfying top-p plausibility constraints across multiple modern open-weight LLMs (Llama-3.2, Gemma-3, Ministral-8B).

Constructive and actionable mechanism design proposal: The proposed pay-per-character mechanism directly addresses the issue, proves incentive compatibility, and includes thoughtful discussion of implementation nuances (such as calibrating character prices to maintain expected revenue parity and incentivizing tokenizer compression).
weaknesses: Practical detectability and external auditability: While the heuristic ensures top-p plausibility under a forward pass check, the paper does not extensively address how easily a client could detect anomalous token fragmentation using statistical anomaly detection (e.g., tracking characters-per-token distributions against canonical BPE tokenization) or standard client-side tokenizers.

Dependence on high-temperature regimes: The financial gains of the plausible overcharging heuristic are modest at standard greedy or low-temperature settings (e.g., around 0.3% at p=0.9 and lower temperatures), achieving substantial gains primarily at elevated temperatures (1.3–1.45) where next-token distributions are sufficiently broad.

Scope limited to output tokens: The paper focuses exclusively on output token pricing, whereas real-world LLM APIs charge for both prompt (input) and completion (output) tokens, with distinct cost structures and potential strategic dynamics for input pre-filling.

strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: The paper connects mechanism design / principal-agent theory with LLM serving economics and tokenization ambiguity, addressing an under-explored vulnerability in current pay-per-token API business models.

Solid theoretical foundations: Theorem 3 provides a clean NP-hardness reduction from Hamiltonian Path for finding the longest plausible token sequence under top-p, top-k, and sequence probability constraints, while Theorem 6 formally characterizes additive incentive-compatible mechanisms as linear in character count.

Feasible proof-of-concept attack: Algorithm 1 presents a lightweight, practically motivated heuristic based on BPE token indices that checks plausibility in a single parallelized forward pass, demonstrating empirical overcharging gains (up to ~13%) under permissive sampling parameters.

Constructive remedy and insightful discussion: The paper does not merely point out an attack; it proposes an incentive-compatible pay-per-character mechanism, discusses practical migration strategies (normalizing via average characters-per-token), and highlights positive structural incentives (encouraging inference compression and energy efficiency).
weaknesses: Gap between the assumed auditability model and real-world API verification: In practice, users can independently run the model's deterministic canonical tokenizer (e.g., standard greedy BPE via Tiktoken or HuggingFace tokenizers) on the returned string. If the contract requires canonical tokenization, any deviation is immediately detectable without needing model logits. The paper's threat model assumes users only audit plausibility via next-token distributions rather than canonical tokenizer execution.

Practical gains diminish under standard generation settings: The empirical overcharging gains rely heavily on elevated temperatures (e.g., T = 1.3 to 1.45) and broad sampling thresholds (p = 0.99). Under typical production configurations (e.g., T <= 0.7, p = 0.90), the overcharging potential drops sharply to <= 0.3%, limiting the real-world financial exploitability.

Provider cost mismatch under pay-per-character pricing: While pay-per-character eliminates token-inflation moral hazard, LLM serving costs scale directly with autoregressive token decoding steps (FLOPs and KV-cache footprint), not character length. Transitioning to per-character billing shifts substantial risk to providers for languages or formats with poor token compression (e.g., non-Latin scripts, code, specialized notation), which warrants deeper economic analysis.

Theoretical reduction relies on unconstrained distributions: The NP-hardness construction constructs an artificial vocabulary and transition structure mapped to graph paths, which deviates substantially from the smooth, semantic probability manifolds produced by actual pretrained language models.

strengths: Original and timely formulation: The paper formalizes the economic relationship between LLM providers and users as a principal-agent problem and uncovers a fundamental moral hazard vulnerability arising from the non-uniqueness of tokenization under pay-per-token pricing.

Rigorous theoretical analysis: The authors provide a clean NP-hardness proof reducing from the directed Hamiltonian path problem to show that finding the optimal plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k sampling is computationally hard, alongside a solid characterization of incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanisms.

Comprehensive empirical proof-of-concept and cost-benefit analysis: The paper demonstrates that a simple token-splitting heuristic (Algorithm 2) can successfully find plausible longer tokenizations. Crucially, the authors measure actual GPU energy consumption (via pynvml on A100/H100 hardware) to prove that the revenue gain outweighs the energy cost of verification forward passes.

Actionable policy and fairness implications: The work proposes a clear formula for transitioning from pay-per-token to pay-per-character while preserving average profit margins, and provides insightful analysis into how pay-per-character naturally mitigates pricing disparities against non-English languages.
weaknesses: Practical effectiveness limited at standard sampling temperatures: As shown in Figures 5-7, the heuristic's success rate and resulting utility gain drop markedly as the temperature decreases towards 1.0 and below (e.g., T=1.15, p=0.90 yields <0.5% gain). Since many real-world API queries are executed with lower temperatures (e.g., T=0.2 to 0.7 for coding or reasoning tasks), the attack vector is primarily impactful in high-entropy/creative generation settings.

Isolation from production serving dynamics: The energy and compute cost modeling assumes isolated single-instance forward passes on single GPUs. In production environments utilizing dynamic batching, paged attention, and continuous batching, the marginal server cost of performing an extra verification forward pass versus serving another concurrent request might introduce different trade-offs.

Relative simplicity of the mechanism design result: While Theorem 6 and Proposition 5 are conceptually elegant and provide a clean normative benchmark, the mathematical derivation of character-count linearity is quite direct once token-invariance is established.

strengths: Novel and insightful perspective: The paper identifies and formalizes a previously overlooked vulnerability in LLM-as-a-service pricing—namely, that pay-per-token pricing creates moral hazard via tokenization misreporting without changing output text.

Solid theoretical foundation: The authors rigorously formulate the principal-agent setting, prove NP-hardness for optimal plausible misreporting via a clean reduction to Hamiltonian path (under top-p, top-k, and threshold settings), and elegantly characterize all incentive-compatible additive pricing mechanisms (Theorem 6).

Thorough empirical analysis and cost accounting: The authors do not just claim theoretical vulnerability; they implement a practical heuristic (Algorithm 2), validate it across multiple model families (Llama, Gemma, Ministral) on LMSYS prompts, and explicitly measure GPU energy consumption (via pynvml) to prove that the verification pass is economically cost-effective.

Practical solution and equitable implications: The proposed pay-per-character mechanism offers a concrete remedy, complete with a calibration rule to maintain average profit margins, and highlights positive equity implications for non-English languages.
weaknesses: Reliance on high-entropy decoding settings: The empirical success of Algorithm 2 relies heavily on elevated sampling temperatures (T = 1.30, 1.45) and broad top-p cutoffs (p = 0.95, 0.99). Under standard default settings (e.g., T = 0.7 or greedy decoding), token plausibility sets are much narrower, significantly diminishing the viability of splitting tokens without detection.

Practical detectability and streaming constraints: In real-world deployment, many API users stream outputs token-by-token or would notice unusual subword fragmentation (e.g., splitting common words like 'simpl-ified' or 'soci-etal') if doing any rudimentary client-side token count inspection against standard public tokenizers.

Nuances of character definition across modalities/scripts: While pay-per-character solves the incentive misalignment nicely in theory, characters are not uniformly defined across Unicode encodings (e.g., multi-byte UTF-8 graphemes vs. codepoints vs. bytes). A deeper discussion of byte- vs. character-level billing in multilingual settings would strengthen the proposal.

strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: The paper formalizes the economic interaction between cloud LLM providers and users as a principal-agent problem, uncovering a fundamental moral hazard inherent to the pay-per-token paradigm due to the non-uniqueness of string tokenization.

Solid theoretical framework: The paper provides rigorous theoretical results, including an NP-hardness proof (Theorem 3) establishing that finding the optimal plausible tokenization under top-p/top-k filtering is computationally hard, and an axiomatic characterization (Theorem 6) proving that any additive incentive-compatible mechanism must price linearly on character counts.

Grounded empirical analysis: The authors validate their findings using real open-weight LLMs (Llama-3.2, Gemma-3, Ministral-8B) on LMSYS Chatbot Arena prompts. Crucially, the paper includes empirical GPU power and energy profiling (using pynvml), demonstrating that the verification cost of the heuristic is low enough to make strategic overcharging financially profitable under high-temperature regimes.

Thoughtful discussion on linguistic fairness: The analysis of pay-per-character across different languages (Appendix C.4) highlights meaningful real-world implications, specifically how pay-per-character helps mitigate the well-documented tokenization tax paid by users of non-English/minority languages.
weaknesses: Vulnerability depends heavily on high sampling temperatures: The empirical profitability of Algorithm 2 relies on high temperatures (e.g., T = 1.3, T = 1.45) and loose top-p thresholds (p = 0.99). In typical real-world enterprise applications (e.g., code generation, structured extraction, factual Q&A), models are queried with T in [0, 0.7], where top-p sets are tight and alternative tokenizations quickly become non-plausible, causing the overcharging margin to drop near zero.

Realism of the adversarial threat model: In practice, an unfaithful provider seeking to maximize revenue can inflate billable tokens far more easily and stealthily by prompting the model to be verbose or padding hidden chain-of-thought tokens, rather than fine-tuning subword token segmentations that risk detection or require forward-pass verification.

Inconsistency in hardware reporting: Appendix A states that all experiments were conducted on a server with Nvidia A100 (80GB) GPUs, whereas Appendix C.3 (Figure 11 and Table 1 caption) explicitly states that energy measurements were conducted on a single Nvidia H100. This inconsistency should be clarified.

Simplicity of the incentive-compatibility result: While Theorem 6 and Corollary 7 are conceptually appealing, their mathematical deduction is relatively straightforward once additivity and single-character token availability are assumed.
